title: When Everything Becomes a Child
author: Samuel J. Abrams
summary: Sarah Lawrence political scientist Samuel Abrams reports a trend among his college students who talk about 'my daughter' or 'my child' while meaning a pet or even a sourdough starter that will not rise. As a father, he first feels anger and then concern about what this language says about how young adults understand family and children. He cites Pew data that 97 percent of pet owners consider pets family while fertility falls and nearly half of childless adults under 50 say they will probably never have children, and wonders whether young people invest affection in animals because children feel out of reach financially. Research by Volsche, Laurent-Simpson and an IFS nine-country survey suggests pet parenthood is associated with wanting fewer children, though causation is unclear. Abrams insists a beloved pet is not a child, and calls for making parenthood more feasible and for adults to speak proudly about its joys, since communal support increases the likelihood of wanting and having children.
points: Students increasingly describe pets and even objects in the language of parenthood, which signals shifting norms about family and children.
Pet ownership is nearly universal as family (97 percent in Pew data) while fertility declines and more childless adults say they will never have children.
Young adults who say they would rather be pet parents want nearly one fewer child, though the direction of causation is unknown.
Affordability, housing and job insecurity may push affection toward animals because children seem out of reach.
Older adults should speak honestly about the joys as well as the costs of parenting and build communal support, which raises the chance young adults want and have children.
quotes: In this one particularly memorable conversation, a student mentioning her daughter’s developmental delays eventually made it clear that her “daughter” was a sourdough starter that wasn’t rising!

How have we reached a point in our society where norms and familial ordering have changed so much that intelligent young people are speaking about pets and children as though the distinction hardly matters?
A 2023 Pew Research Center survey found that 97% of American pet owners consider their pets part of the family, and 51% say they are as much a part of the family as a human member.
I wonder if young people are investing affection in animals—or things—because having children seems so out of reach.
Young adults who agreed with the statement “I would rather be a pet parent” reported wanting nearly one less child than those who did not.

I wish more of my students heard more about the pleasures of parenting, but unfortunately too many have only heard about the hardships. Yes, there is exhaustion and expense, but who is telling them how wonderful having children can be?
A pet can be beloved without being a child, and no amount of affection for an animal can replace the kind of joy and meaning in life that a child brings.
